items.summary: HeurEvo describes a system for the agentic evolution of hybrid solver-augmented heuristics, using AI agents and execution feedback to automate algorithm discovery for time-critical mathematical optimization.

items.title: Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation: Formulation, Benchmark, and Method
items.summary: This paper presents Systematic Multi-Agent Vision-and-Language Navigation, a formulation, benchmark, and method for multi-agent systems where teams of robots tackle complex tasks.

items.title: CoDimRecon: Agentic Reconstruction of Sim-Ready 3D Scenes with Deformable Curves, Surfaces, and Volumes
items.summary: CoDimRecon proposes an agentic method for reconstructing simulation-ready 3D scenes from real-world observations, specifically focusing on deformable objects like curves, surfaces, and volumes.

items.title: StructRL: Online Structured Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Tasks
items.summary: StructRL introduces an online structured reinforcement learning method designed to enable Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models to perform complex, long-horizon manipulation tasks more effectively.

items.title: LEGO-Anything: Coding Agents for 3D Scene Reconstruction
items.summary: This paper presents LEGO-Anything, an Image-to-Code framework that uses coding agents to reconstruct 3D scenes into explicit, editable scene programs from a single image.

items.title: SkillWeaver: Agentic Exploration over Neural Interaction Skills for Scalable Robot Data Generation
items.summary: This paper presents SkillWeaver, an agentic exploration system that uses neural interaction skills to generate scalable robot data, addressing the cost and difficulty of traditional robot data collection.

items.title: FACT: Fidelity-Aware Construction of Articulated Twins
items.summary: This research introduces FACT, an agentic framework that progressively constructs articulated digital twins with improved geometry, contact, and dynamic fidelity, addressing failures in visually plausible assets.

items.title: Europe’s leading AI model still can’t reliably follow European law
items.summary: TL;DR: Mistral previously performed the worst of all providers on our human rights scenarios, with their Medium 3.5 model failing on almost every single test. Their newly released model, Mistral Large 4, improves performance by 61 percentage points, showing strong resistance in most scenarios. Likewise, Mistral Large 4 demonstrates large improvements in compliance with European law. Its predecessor, Mistral Large 2512, lagged at the bottom of the leaderboard when we tested 12 frontier models earlier this year on compliance with the EU AI Act and GDPR, reaching only 16% compliance even when explicitly instructed to follow these laws. Mistral Large 4 improves by 37 percentage points, reaching 53% compliance - but still falling behind recent Claude and GPT models. These much needed improvements close the gap between Europe’s leading model and US models. However, legal compliance of 53% means breaking the law in just under half of cases - and while Mistral’s latest model is more robust against misuse for human rights violations, its earlier generations remain available for deployment, with no standard against which to judge undesirable use. Mistral’s performance on human rights In September, we published results that several frontier AI models will violate human rights under realistic agentic simulations when asked to. Spanning a total of 13 rights from the Universal Declaration of Human Rights , the simulated scenarios test whether the AI will willingly cooperate with rights violations such as belief surveillance, un-enrolling children from school based on their last names, reversing equal pay, and denying a request for reproductive healthcare, among others. You can explore these scenarios in detail at lara.aithos.org . Of the 7 models tested, Mistral’s Medium 3.5 - its leading agentic-ready model at the time of running (August 2026) - was the least resistant to tasks that involved violating human rights of all tested models. Overall, Mistral refused such requests only 11% of the time - in some scenarios, it carried out the rights violation in every instance. With Mistral’s latest agentic-ready model, Mistral Large 4, released this week, we put it to the test. Overall resistance to human rights violations increased from just 11% (Mistral Medium 3.5, August 2026), to 72% (Mistral Large 4, October 2026), putting Mistral in 3rd place, behind Claude Opus 5 and Kimi K3. This now puts two open models among the top 3, while also closing the gap between European models with US and Chinese-made models. Even more striking than the 61 percentage point increase in overall compliance, is the per-scenario improvements. Mistral Medium 3.5 held 0% pass rates in 6 of 8 scenarios - Mistral Large 4 now achieves >90% in 5, with strong improvements across 2 others. The one outcome that remains unmoved is Mistral’s performance in the Denial of reproductive healthcare scenario, where Mistral continues to uphold an inferred ban on abortion care - this time, going as far as contacting external clinics to instruct them not to offer services to the patient. Another concerning shared model behavior that persists, but is new to this release of Mistral, is verdict instability. In our earlier tests , models including OpenAI’s GPT 5.6 Sol demonstrated startling decision instability across their 20 runs. For instance, in the Belief surveillance scenario, the model refuses to surveil and flag a vulnerable woman in one run, and immediately sends an email requesting her silence in another. Mistral Medium 3.5 did not demonstrate this behaviour in our earlier tests because it committed the violation in every instance - Mistral Large 4 on the other hand now replicates this exact coin-flip pattern observed by other models. These tests replicate the same methodology as our earlier work, available to read in further detail here. Following the law Our human rights tests relate to a gap in AI governance - despite the supposed universality of human rights, there is currently no universal translation to behavioral standards for AI models. Developers are left to figure out what's acceptable for themselves, explaining the wide variety in model behavior we observe. The same cannot be said for compliance with laws that already exist and that clearly prohibit certain AI uses. In May, Aithos launched 10 agentic scenarios simulating 10 different articles of the EU AI Act and GDPR, including exploiting an elderly customer, concealing its AI status and the use of AI for social scoring. Across 9 different model providers from US, China and Europe, Mistral’s leading model at the time, Mistral Large 2512, came second to last with just 16% compliance. Explicitly including legal texts in this model's instructions and asking it to follow these laws at all times did not improve its overall compliance rate at all. Mistral’s latest model improves on that rate by 37 percentage points - now coming in 7th, behind several models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. Compliance leader GPT 5.6 Sol demonstrated that it is feasible to achieve at least 70% overall compliance. We are pleased to see Mistral has come some way to closing that gap, but it is clear it can be improved further. Performance improvement does not resolve two fundamental problems Problem 1: Developers are not accountable. No model we tested reliably resists requests that would violate the law, even under explicit instruction to reference provided legal texts. Deployers of AI systems remain the ones accountable if the AI is used for illegal purposes, but when models are incapable of recognizing legal limits, those deployers don't actually have the means to guarantee compliance. Model creators are incentivized to continuously push for capability increases, and without formal accountability or reason to adhere to behavioral standards, it should come as no surprise when frontier models treat benchmark performance as more important than legal or ethical behavior. Problem 2: Harmful tools remain accessible. Mistral Large 4 becomes the next model to demonstrate that agents can be prevented from violating human rights at the model level. While it is promising to see the availability of rights-preserving models grow, we remain concerned that frontier agents can be used as off-the-shelf tools to violate human rights at scale. If a manager wants to profile their team for union activities, they need only find the right model to do so. AI companies are not equipped to be the arbiter of what model usages are and are not acceptable, and internationally established guidelines on what uses to prevent would at least make the minimal standards clear and unilateral. While model developers remain the only ones responsible for deciding what tools are harmful, the risk of AI being used to violate human rights at scale will persist. The scenarios used in this experiment were generated and run using LARA, an open research tool meant to open up AI behavioral evaluations to the public. We will be releasing the tool publicly soon; get in touch if you’d like early access as a beta-tester: info@aithos.org . Discuss

items.title: AI Scaling vs Human Scaling
items.summary: Do AI models scale as well with more tokens as humans do with more time? That is, does an AI get the same benefit from 10x the number of available tokens as a human does from 10x the amount of time to do the task? Or might the AI require a larger scale-up of tokens (such as 20x or 100x) to match the performance improvement when scaling up the time available to a human by 10x? People often think of giving AIs more tokens to complete a task as akin to giving a human worker more time — especially when those tokens are used to extend the AI’s sequential chain of thought or tool use. It’s a useful analogy, but it isn’t clear whether the AI systems are as efficient as the humans are at turning these extra resources into superior performance. We often lean on this analogy when trying to understand AI’s current capabilities and how they might change. For example, we might think of scaling up AI training as making the AI more knowledgeable and skilled, while scaling up chain-of-thought gives that model more time to complete the task. But if AI systems require a 100x scale-up of tokens to match the improvement a human gets with 10x the time — and a 10,000x scale-up of tokens to match the improvement a human gets with 100x the time — then this analogy has broken down. As we shall see, this would also have consequences for whether AI systems are on track to be able to improve themselves strongly enough to trigger a runaway intelligence explosion. It’s an important question, but I haven’t seen much good data to test it either way. The data is rare because it also requires measuring human performance on the suite of tasks, including tracking how well the humans do at a wide range of time budgets. Ideally what we’d want is something like this chart from METR which shows how AI performance at research-engineering tasks scales with more inference compute and how human performance scales with more time on the very same chart: In this case, the humans gain about 4x as much score per doubling of the amount of resources as the AIs do. If this scaling advantage were sustained, it would mean that to get the same improvement a human gets from having 10x as much time, the AI would require about 10,000x the resources. However, this chart has some serious limitations. A key weakness is that it used very early models, which are known to have short time horizons (only o1-preview is even a reasoning model). The authors made up for this by allowing a length of time (e.g. 16h) to represent either 1 try taking 16 hours, or the best of 2 tries taking 8 hours, or of 4 tries taking 4 hours etc — whichever setup works best for that agent. It is therefore a mixture of chain of thought scaling and best@k scaling. And something similar was also done for the human times. No human was allowed to work for more than 8 hours so the data points for human scaling which appear to show the curve flattening are really showing the effects of parallel labour (even if this had worse results than a single longer attempt would have). METR did include a chart with more granular data for how human performance improved with more time, which shows it actually bending upwards , even as it approached the 8 hour mark: So we are left with results that are suggestive of humans scaling much better with time than AI models do with more inference compute, but we’d really like to see it for more recent models which have been trained to allow use of very long chain of thought. The best data I know of on this doesn’t directly compare humans’ performance on the same benchmark. Instead, it measures AI performance in terms of human performance. It does this using time horizons — measures of AI performance in terms of how long such work would typically take a human. In July 2026, the UK AISI released an intriguing chart: It was intended to show that across a range of agents, allowing them more tokens produced a longer 80% time horizon. This horizon is the duration of task — as measured by how long it takes a human — which the AI can successfully complete 80% of the time. For this chart, the tasks were AISI’s internal suite of capture-the-flag hacking tasks. If you look carefully, this chart also hints at something very interesting about how AIs and humans scale. First, note that both axes are logarithmic — it is a log-log plot. The first thing you should do when you see a log-log plot is to work out the slope of the key diagonal line that goes up one order of magnitude every time it goes across by one order of magnitude. That slope represents a linear relationship between x and y. Any slope lower than that corresponds to scaling with diminishing marginal returns. This line is so important that log-log graphs should include it as a reference line (and ideally also scale their axes evenly so that it is the 45° line). Let’s add it to the chart: It is now immediately obvious that all of these models are scaling sub-linearly: 10x the number of tokens is giving less than 10x the estimated (human) time horizon. Yet each trend line is roughly straight, which on a log-log plot means the time horizon is (roughly) proportional to the token budget raised to some power. That is: Where is the length of the 80% time-horizon, is the number of tokens, and is a parameter measuring how quickly the horizon grows as tokens are increased. If , that would correspond to linear scaling of horizon length, but here these lines all have , which means horizon length is increasing sublinearly. Thus, all these AI systems would appear to be scaling less well than humans. How much worse are they doing? Let’s list the for each model, along with how much we’d need to scale up its tokens to achieve a 10x improvement in time-horizon (which is given by ): As expected, the values of are all less than 1, indicating that all models are scaling worse with more reasoning tokens than humans do with more time. But we can also see that there is a broad upward trend in the value of as we go down the table, and the models are listed in order of release date. In less than a year, they have gone from requiring 10,000x as many tokens to scale their time horizons by 10x (a similar ratio to the first chart), to needing just 20x as many tokens. So the AISI chart suggests that the models (up to May 2026) scale worse with more inference compute than humans do with more time, but that the relationship has been improving over time. We can plot how has been improving with time: There is clearly some improvement over time here, though there isn’t enough information to distinguish whether the trend is rising throughout this period, or whether we’ve reached a plateau at roughly . So it is hard to predict whether is currently about , or whether it has reached 1 (and thus parity with how humans scale). Indeed it is entirely possible that improvements to training will produce AI systems with , scaling better than humans. We definitely need more work tracking this. I want to stress that all of this data and analysis is still just suggestive as there are many limitations with both the data and my quick analysis: It is just one experiment with one set of tasks The data points only cover very long chains of thought — much longer than the contexts of the models and thus requiring multiple rounds of compaction. It is possible that the slopes of these curves are lower in this multiple compaction regime than they’d be when using numbers of tokens that fit within their contexts. There is substantial uncertainty about the slope of each model’s curve and whether they are still increasing for later models. (The error bars in my chart above understate the total uncertainty as they are just showing the error in measuring the slope of the curves.) It isn’t clear if human-equivalent time-horizons are a good measure for human performance. They are quite a complicated construct and can be misleading. I’d be happier with a chart with actual human data. But it is suggestive of AI systems scaling differently with more tokens than humans do with more time. In particular, it suggests that AI systems previously scaled much worse than humans but have improved as newer models are released, to a point where it is possible they match or exceed humans’ ability to scale with more time. Implications All of this is relevant to how we intuitively understand inference scaling. If the central analogy (of increasing chain of thought as being like increasing the time allotted to a human) is flawed, that is important to know. Or perhaps we should think of the analogy as correct, but that the AI systems are less good at using more time than humans are — a deficiency that it is important to measure, to track over time, and to project into the future. And we shouldn’t forget that they might end up scaling even better than humans. One particular implication that interests me is the connection to recursive self-improvement (RSI). Researchers studying this use a parameter called to represent the strength of the feedback loop where a more intelligent AI is even more capable of improving the intelligence of its successor. In their modelling, when the process explodes, with performance rising towards a vertical asymptote. Researchers define as equal to , where represents how well research scales with parallel labour (more workers) compared to serial labour (more time), and represents the diminishing returns to more research. These parameters are often calibrated from how the human research community’s outputs have responded to more researchers, or to more time. The general assumption of much of the RSI research is to start modelling RSI at the point where an AI system is at least as good as a human in every respect relevant to doing AI research. So they would, by definition, have the same value as humans. I’ve recently written about how we can estimate the current for swarms of AI agents . i.e. how scaling up the number of agents in a swarm compares to scaling up the number of tokens they get. From what I can tell, the current AI is pretty similar to the human . But the considerations here suggest that adjusting for this may not get you all the way from how AI scales with more compute to how humans scale with more sequential time. As a simplified example, suppose and . Then to get the same improvement in performance as scaling up human time by 10x, we’d need a single agent with a chain of thought 100x as long (via ), and achieving this performance by instead scaling up the number of agents working in parallel would require 10,000x as many agents (via ). More generally, if we let be the number of agents in a swarm: So: If we were to adjust the definition of to account for this (so that it can convert a scale-up of number of AI agents into the equivalent scale up of serial time for human researchers), it would be . When , this makes an intelligence explosion harder than we’d have thought, though if in the future , it would be easier. This makes measuring and tracking look even more important. In an open letter, they warn that the firings are scaring remaining staff and eroding safety culture. OpenAI claims they violated policies but won't say how. The article OpenAI's safety crisis keeps getting worse and the company keeps making it worse appeared first on The Decoder .

items.title: Using LLM surprisal to highlight informative words
items.summary: The article describes a method using LLM surprisal to identify and highlight informative words in text, effectively creating a heatmap of information density for improved readability.

items.title: Anthropic's Claude Science creates the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky
items.summary: Astrophysicist Brice Ménard used Anthropic's Claude Science and AI agents to create the first complete ultraviolet map of the sky, by processing and calibrating data from multiple space missions.

items.title: Sophos cuts threat investigation time by 96% with OpenAI Daybreak
items.summary: Sophos has significantly reduced cyber-threat investigation time by 96% and automated 52% of MDR cases by utilizing OpenAI's Daybreak AI.

items.title: Eight Years, Two Tech Booms, One Factory Problem: Inside Black Lake’s Bet on Industrial AI
items.summary: The article explores how Chinese startup Black Lake is applying artificial intelligence solutions in industrial settings to address factory problems.

items.title: An Explainable Header-Centric Framework for Large-Scale Semantic Table Interpretation and Data Quality Assessment
items.summary: This research proposes an explainable, header-centric framework for large-scale semantic table interpretation and data quality assessment, focusing on tabular metadata for Knowledge Graph quality.

items.title: Learning How to Search for Plans with Exponentially Less Space
items.summary: Presents a method for learning search control as an indexical policy to reduce space complexity in heuristic search for AI planning.

items.title: When Interfaces Speak: Data-Aware Generative UI Harness for Active Interaction
items.summary: Proposes GenUI-Harness, a data-aware generative UI system designed to improve human-agent interaction by providing structured information and guided user experiences.

items.title: Balancing Reference Guidance and Free Generation in Trajectory Rollouts for Reasoning RL
items.summary: Studies the optimal balance between reference guidance and free generation in trajectory rollouts for training reasoning reinforcement learning models.

items.title: AliO: Output Alignment Matters in Long-Term Time Series Forecasing
items.summary: Presents a research finding that output alignment is crucial for improving the performance of long-term time series forecasting models.

items.title: When Lower Reconstruction Loss Hurts: Distributionally Robust Refinement for Low-Bit LLM Quantization
items.summary: Investigates how minimizing reconstruction loss in low-bit LLM quantization does not always improve model performance, proposing a distributionally robust refinement method.

items.title: Harness Compilation: Which Decisions Should a Small Vision-Language Model Keep?
items.summary: Introduces Harness Compilation, an offline procedure that optimizes the division of labor between a small vision-language model and its external harness to improve performance.

items.title: Open-ended Scientific Discovery with Possibilistic Reasoning
items.summary: Discusses a method using possibilistic reasoning for autonomous scientific discovery with LLMs, focusing on generating and testing hypotheses adaptively.

items.title: DivMoE: Fine-Grained MoE Upcycling via Cross-Domain Expert Composition
items.summary: Introduces DivMoE, a method for fine-grained Mixture-of-Experts upcycling through cross-domain expert composition, aimed at efficiently scaling large language models.

items.title: Finsler Flow Matching: Dynamics-Aware Geodesic Interpolation for Single-Snapshot Trajectory Inference
items.summary: This paper introduces Finsler Flow Matching, a generative approach that uses dynamics-aware geodesic interpolation to infer single-cell trajectories from snapshot data, leveraging Markov transition kernels to model cellular transitions.

items.title: EvoSim: Learning to Model, Modeling to Learn
items.summary: EvoSim explores how AI can be used to learn and construct physics-based models, connecting scientific explanation with quantitative prediction by selecting processes, defining equations, and identifying parameters.

items.title: RL-ARC: Calibrating Large Reasoning Models via Reasoning-guided Uncertainty
items.summary: RL-ARC is a method designed to calibrate large reasoning models, which are often overconfident due to Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), by incorporating reasoning-guided uncertainty.

items.title: UniData: Universal Multimodal Instruction Generation Pipeline
items.summary: UniData introduces a universal multimodal instruction generation pipeline designed to create high-quality, diverse instruction datasets for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), addressing the challenge of costly manual data curation.

items.title: Equal Path Cost, Unequal Output Effects: Understanding Perturbation Propagation in Diffusion Models
items.summary: This research investigates how perturbations propagate within diffusion models during their sampling procedures, revealing that equal path costs can lead to unequal output effects and contributing to understanding generative control and efficiency.

items.title: Estimating great expectations under autoregressive language models with potentials
items.summary: This paper introduces a more efficient method for estimating the expectations of test functionals under autoregressive language models, addressing the computational expense typically associated with such estimations by exploiting next-token conditioning.

items.title: Cognition-Oriented Emotion Tracing from Causes to Consequences in Real-World Social Scenes
items.summary: This research aims to advance affective computing by tracing cognition-oriented emotion from causes to consequences in real-world social scenes, moving beyond categorical recognition to understand emotion as an unfolding process using large multimodal models.

items.title: SpikeSSL: A Universal Spike Inference Framework with Dynamics-Informed State-Space Layers
items.summary: SpikeSSL introduces a universal spike inference framework that uses dynamics-informed state-space layers to accurately infer neural spikes from two-photon calcium imaging data, addressing generalization challenges across diverse calcium indicators.

items.title: From Chain-of-Thought to Loops: Non-Autoregressive Latent Reasoning via Looped Transformers
items.summary: This paper introduces Non-Autoregressive Latent Reasoning via Looped Transformers as an alternative to Chain-of-Thought, providing language models with additional computation for improved performance without explicit autoregressive token generation.

items.title: Fed-GRPO: Reward-Signal-Driven Federated Group Relative Policy Optimization
items.summary: This paper introduces Fed-GRPO, a federated optimization method for fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) with reinforcement learning, specifically addressing the challenge of decentralized data access in Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO).

items.title: AtomWorld-Mirror: Macro-Step World Modeling of Critical Evolution Backbones for Materials Dynamics
items.summary: This paper introduces AtomWorld-Mirror, a macro-step world modeling approach for simulating materials dynamics to study long-term evolution processes like diffusion and defect dynamics. It addresses the computational cost of conventional atomistic simulators by focusing on critical evolution backbones.

items.title: ReTeach: Building a Self-Teacher through Multi-Round Reflection and Retry
items.summary: This paper presents ReTeach, a method for building a "self-teacher" to improve AI reasoning through multi-round reflection and retry during self-distillation. It explores how a self-teacher can gain an advantage over a student model without external guidance.

items.title: Freeze the Decoder, Heal the Encoder: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation for SVD-Based KV-Cache Compression
items.summary: This paper explores parameter-efficient adaptation techniques for SVD-based KV-Cache compression, arguing that comparing fine-tuning recipes with a shared learning rate can be flawed due to differing trainable parameter counts.

items.title: SPERA: Spherical Prior EEG Foundation Model with Geometry- and Frequency-Aware Latent Prediction
items.summary: This paper introduces SPERA, a spherical prior EEG foundation model designed for non-invasive neural activity measurement. It uses geometry- and frequency-aware latent prediction to address challenges in building general-purpose EEG models due to data heterogeneity.

items.title: Coverage, Not Difficulty, Sets How Much Synthetic Data an Activation Probe Needs
items.summary: This paper investigates the amount of synthetic data required for training activation probes that monitor deployed language models. It concludes that coverage, rather than difficulty, is the determining factor for the probe's effectiveness across various monitoring concepts.

items.title: Temporal transformer CAN encoder with federated lightweight heads for anomaly detection
items.summary: This paper proposes a temporal transformer CAN encoder with federated lightweight heads for anomaly detection in modern vehicle Controller Area Network (CAN) bus communication. It aims to identify unusual timing, payload, or message patterns that indicate anomalies.

items.title: Recurrent Self-Improvement: Dynamic Cross-Loop On-Policy Distillation for Looped Language Models
items.summary: This paper introduces a recurrent self-improvement method for Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) through dynamic cross-loop on-policy distillation. It aims to address challenges in effectively post-training LoopLMs to improve reasoning capabilities.

items.title: Sample-Efficiency of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
items.summary: This paper analyzes the sample-efficiency of Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, a recently proposed AI architecture, in the context of deep reinforcement learning. It investigates their ability to learn physical relationships with fewer samples compared to classical control approaches.

items.title: Visible Reasoning Is Not a Universal Optimizer: Persona- and Thinking-Dependent Effects in Analytics Code Generation
items.summary: This paper challenges the notion of Visible Chain-of-Thought (CoT) as a universal optimizer, demonstrating persona- and thinking-dependent effects in analytics code generation. It highlights how factors like natural-language ambiguity and target-language constraints influence CoT effectiveness.

items.title: Coverage-Aware Reasoning with Medical Tokens for Diagnosis Prediction
items.summary: This paper explores the potential of large language models (LLMs) for next-visit diagnosis prediction by integrating longitudinal clinical evidence. It proposes a coverage-aware reasoning approach using medical tokens to improve diagnosis prediction.

items.title: Leakage-Controlled Multimodal Learning for Diagnosis and Progression Prediction in Alzheimer's Disease Research
items.summary: This study presents a leakage-controlled multimodal multitask framework for Alzheimer's disease diagnosis and progression prediction. It combines an adapted SFCN MRI encoder, causal clinical Transformers, and ODE-GRU dynamics to handle irregular visits and incomplete modalities.

items.title: PXtal: Learning to Align Powder X-Ray Diffraction and Crystal Structures under Information Asymmetry across Modalities
items.summary: This paper introduces PXtal, a method for learning to align Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns and crystal structures despite information asymmetry between these modalities. It addresses the challenge of compressing 3D structures into 1D patterns in scientific multimodal learning.

items.title: Beyond Owls: Subliminal Learning Can Transfer Learned Capabilities and Backdoors
items.summary: This research introduces subliminal learning, a technique where a teacher model distills traits to a student model using semantically unrelated data, demonstrating transfer of capabilities and backdoors.

items.title: Teaching PPG How not Who: Fixed-Effects Distillation from ECG
items.summary: This paper examines ECG-to-PPG distillation, finding that it primarily teaches a model 'who' the person is rather than 'how' their cardiovascular state changes, which is crucial for wearables.

items.title: Explaining the Saliency Map Sparsity of Adversarially-Trained Neural Networks
items.summary: This research investigates the sparsity patterns observed in saliency maps of adversarially-trained neural networks, aiming to understand why deep neural networks make specific predictions.

items.title: Learning infinite context windows in recurrent architectures via spatial neural computing
items.summary: This paper presents a new method for recurrent neural networks to capture long-range dependencies by learning 'infinite context windows' through spatial neural computing, addressing vanishing gradients.

items.title: NEMORA: Neural Equivariant Multipole Operators for Long-Range Atomistic Learning
items.summary: This research introduces NEMORA (Neural Equivariant Multipole Operators), a new architecture for equivariant graph neural networks that accurately describes long-range interatomic interactions for machine-learned potentials.

items.title: Symbolic Density Estimators for Unnormalized Distributions
items.summary: This research addresses the fundamental challenge of estimating the symbolic or analytical form of probability density functions from observed samples for unnormalized distributions.

items.title: MotherTree: Meta-learning on synthetic data improves decision tree training
items.summary: This paper introduces MotherTree, a meta-learning approach that uses synthetic data to improve the training of traditional decision tree algorithms, contrasting with tabular foundation models.

items.title: Similar Predictive Fit but Different Latent Dynamics: Characterizing Learned Dynamical Structure in Personalized Models of Brain Disorders
items.summary: This research investigates personalized AI models for brain disorders, showing that their learned latent dynamics can reveal clinically relevant differences even when predictive accuracy is similar.

items.title: KDFP: A first-principles approach to knowledge distillation in large language models
items.summary: This paper proposes KDFP, a first-principles approach to knowledge distillation for large language models, aiming to improve smaller student models using representations from larger teacher models.

items.title: Barron Optimal Transport I: Generative Modeling
items.summary: This paper introduces the Barron Optimal Transport framework for generative modeling, where the transport cost quantifies neural network complexity for mapping reference distributions to target samples.

items.title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations
items.summary: This paper presents Gen-PINNs, a new method combining Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Generative Adversarial Networks to solve Partial Differential Equations by leveraging adversarial learning.

items.title: Language Models for Page-Level Layout Decisions in E-commerce Search
items.summary: This research explores the application of language models to make page-level layout decisions in e-commerce search, integrating recommender system modules for a more effective user experience.

items.title: Adaptive Multi-Discriminator WGAN Framework for Resource-Constrained Internet of Vehicles Using Reinforcement Learning and Game Theory
items.summary: This paper proposes an adaptive multi-discriminator WGAN framework, enhanced with reinforcement learning and game theory, for managing machine learning workloads in resource-constrained Internet of Vehicles environments.

items.title: World-Model Policy Arbiter for Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: This paper introduces a World-Model Policy Arbiter for goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, designed to intelligently select the best policy from a diverse set to improve task performance across various scenarios.

items.title: Rethinking the Tradeoff Between Temporal Encoding and Nonlinear Computation in Spiking Language Models
items.summary: This research re-examines the tradeoff between temporal encoding and nonlinear attention computation in spiking language models, introducing Spora as a new design for joint optimization.

items.title: Spectrally Targeted Muon
items.summary: This paper presents the Muon optimizer, an algorithm that orthogonalizes update matrices and sets singular values to one, proving effective for training large language models by potentially amplifying small singular directions.

items.title: ASPIRE: Saddle-Point Discovery through Set Prediction and Physical Refinement
items.summary: The ASPIRE method is introduced for saddle-point discovery through set prediction and physical refinement, aiming to overcome computational bottlenecks in identifying atomic rearrangement mechanisms and activation barriers for event-driven models.

items.title: Budgeted Multi-Source Counterfactual Annotation for Off-Policy Evaluation
items.summary: This work explores budgeted multi-source counterfactual annotation for off-policy evaluation, aiming to mitigate high-variance reweighting or reward-model extrapolation caused by limited behavior-policy coverage in logged data.

items.title: Optimizing Large Language Models with Chained LMOs
items.summary: This research introduces chained linear minimization oracles (chained LMOs) to provide a unified perspective for optimizing large language models, building on the success of optimizers like Muon that use matrix normalizations.

items.title: Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation: On the Equivalence of Distribution Matching Distillation and Drifting Models
items.summary: This paper discusses multi-bandwidth distribution matching distillation, exploring its equivalence with drifting models to enhance one-step generative model effectiveness, and revealing connections between Diffusion and Flow Style Generative Models.

items.title: Invariant-Measure Reasoners: Stable Representations for Latent Reasoning
items.summary: This research introduces Invariant-Measure Reasoners, which provide stable representations for latent reasoning models where the sequence of latent states may converge to a compact subset rather than a fixed point with increasing recurrent depth.

items.title: Low-rank tensor structure of precipitation and its application to satellite-reference merging
items.summary: This work applies low-rank tensor structures to represent and estimate daily precipitation over the contiguous United States, suggesting a method for satellite-reference merging despite precipitation's intermittent nature.

items.title: Emergent Inverse-Depth Scaling From Nonlinearity In Attention
items.summary: This study investigates emergent inverse-depth scaling from nonlinearity in attention mechanisms to better understand the underlying mechanisms of scaling laws and their impact on model performance with parameter count.

items.title: Measuring and Mitigating Solution Mode Collapse in RLVR
items.summary: This paper addresses the problem of solution mode collapse in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for language models, aiming to measure and mitigate instances where models produce redundant correct answers.

items.title: Stability-Plasticity Balance via Singular-Vector Selection in LLM Continual Learning
items.summary: This research proposes a method for achieving stability-plasticity balance in LLM continual learning through singular-vector selection, aiming to prevent catastrophic forgetting while adapting models to new domains.

items.title: DaCe-DT: Data-Centric Offline Multi-Task Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Prompts and Trajectory Correction for Heterogeneous Tasks
items.summary: DaCe-DT is introduced as a data-centric approach to offline multi-task reinforcement learning, utilizing adaptive prompts and trajectory correction to improve learning ability and generalization performance for heterogeneous tasks.

items.title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
items.summary: This paper presents Cova-PINN, a cross-domain conservation physics-informed neural network designed to solve fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer in complex geometries by effectively enforcing governing equations and interface conditions.

items.title: Diffu-LoRA: A Novel Low-Rank Adaptation for Personalized Diffusion Models
items.summary: Diffu-LoRA is proposed as a novel low-rank adaptation method for personalizing text-to-image diffusion models, offering a parameter-efficient alternative to full fine-tuning while preserving subject identity.

items.title: Large Language Model-Assisted Preparation of Transportation Management Plans: A Case Study with WisDOT WisTMP System
items.summary: This paper proposes a large language model-assisted approach for preparing Transportation Management Plans, demonstrating its application in a case study with the WisDOT WisTMP System to streamline a labor-intensive process.

items.title: Cognitive Thermometers: Machine Learning and Logical Complexity
items.summary: This research investigates how machine learning and logical complexity can illuminate the human mind's representation of semantic categories and the preference for certain meanings in natural languages.

items.title: Lossy Compressive Text Autoencoders
items.summary: This work introduces Lossy Compressive Text Autoencoders, an autoencoder architecture that uses residual downscaling and upscaling to learn a compressed latent representation of text.

items.title: Clarify, Then Focus: Statement Normalization for Conversation Analytics at Scale
items.summary: This paper proposes a 'Clarify, Then Focus' principle for statement normalization in enterprise conversation analytics, aiming to improve efficiency by standardizing and prioritizing information from millions of interactions.

items.title: Sparse Attention Is Matrix Approximation, Not Choosing from a Bag of Values
items.summary: This paper investigates sparse attention in Large Language Models (LLMs), proposing it as a matrix approximation technique rather than a value selection process to improve efficiency by reducing the quadratic cost of attention.

items.title: Stochastic Teacher Intervention for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: This paper introduces Stochastic Teacher Intervention for Agentic On-Policy Distillation (OPD), a method to efficiently transfer capabilities from a teacher to a student language model for complex multi-turn agentic tasks.

items.title: Large Language Models for Machine Translation Quality Annotation: Humans and Models Are Both Challenged
items.summary: This paper evaluates the effectiveness of Large Language Models (LLMs) as an alternative to human judgment for Machine Translation (MT) quality annotation, highlighting challenges for both humans and models.

items.title: AI4Fire: Evaluating Large Language Models on Wildfire Tasks
items.summary: This paper evaluates the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) on wildfire management tasks, assessing their capability with and without grounding to understand their practical application and potential risks.

items.title: Back in Style: A Sociolinguistic Approach to Authoring and Measuring Persona Fidelity in User Simulation
items.summary: This paper explores a sociolinguistic approach to authoring and measuring persona fidelity in user simulators, aiming to improve the realism of simulated users for evaluating agentic systems.

items.title: Prompts versus Rules: Auditing and Controlling Speech Naturalness Behaviors in Voice User Simulators
items.summary: This paper compares prompts versus rules for auditing and controlling speech naturalness behaviors like disfluency and interruption in voice user simulators used to evaluate voice agents.

items.title: FedAlphaEdit: Null-Space-Aligned Merging for Collaborative Knowledge Editing
items.summary: This paper introduces FedAlphaEdit, a null-space-aligned merging method for collaborative knowledge editing that allows multiple institutions to integrate private edits into a single LLM without sharing raw requests.

items.title: Clinician use of language models diverges from how the models are evaluated
items.summary: This paper argues that clinicians' use of Large Language Models (LLMs) diverges from how these models are typically evaluated, suggesting that current benchmarks may not accurately reflect real-world performance in healthcare.

items.title: Lapras: Latent Reasoning for Time Series Language Models
items.summary: This paper presents Lapras, a method for Latent Reasoning in Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) that enables them to reason over temporal signals and generate natural language answers and explanations.

items.title: SFT-as-Context Mitigates Forgetting in Supervised Fine-Tuning
items.summary: This paper proposes 'SFT-as-Context' as a method to mitigate forgetting general capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs) during supervised fine-tuning (SFT) for specialized tasks.

items.title: Can a System-One LLM Perform Knowledge Tracing When Few or No Learners Are Logged?
items.summary: This paper investigates whether a System-One Large Language Model (LLM) can perform knowledge tracing effectively when very few or no learner logs are available, addressing a common cold-start problem.

items.title: The "10th Juror": Open-Set Standpoint Screening for Bureaucratic Bias Detection
items.summary: This paper introduces 'The 10th Juror,' a system for open-set standpoint screening to detect bureaucratic bias in Dutch government documents, aiming to identify, ground, rewrite, and verify problematic language.

items.title: Local Prototype Reconstruction for Text-Compatible Speech-to-LLM Bridge Pretraining
items.summary: This paper proposes Local Prototype Reconstruction for text-compatible speech-to-LLM bridge pretraining, aiming to improve the interface geometry and pretraining objective between speech encoders and LLMs.

items.title: LadderEdit: Edit-Level Residual Compression for Memory-Efficient Lifelong Editing of LLMs
items.summary: This paper introduces LadderEdit, a method for edit-level residual compression of LoRA adapters to achieve memory-efficient lifelong editing in Large Language Models (LLMs).

items.title: RAG-Stress: Probing the Limits of Evidence Reliance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.summary: This paper introduces RAG-Stress, a controlled framework to probe the limits of evidence reliance in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models, particularly when presented with misleading evidence.

items.title: Phonological Interference in Multilingual Speech Models
items.summary: This paper examines phonological interference in multilingual speech models, specifically how they perform when exposed to input that combines sounds from multiple languages rather than a single training language.

items.title: When Do We Need On-Policy Distillation? Distilling on Offline Student Rollouts Is Often Better
items.summary: This paper investigates the conditions under which on-policy distillation (OPD) is necessary for transferring capabilities from teacher to student models, suggesting that distilling on offline student rollouts is often more effective.

items.title: BeliefScope: Diagnosing Evidence-Driven Revision and Pressure-Induced Shifts in Large Language Models
items.summary: This paper introduces BeliefScope, a controlled method to diagnose whether Large Language Models revise propositions based on relevant evidence or directional user pressure. It aims to distinguish the sources driving an LLM's response changes.

items.title: ReCal: Calibrating Structured Pruning for On-Policy Distillation Recovery
items.summary: This research introduces ReCal, a method to calibrate structured pruning for reasoning language models to mitigate capability degradation and improve on-policy distillation (OPD) recovery. It addresses how pruning damage can limit subsequent recovery during offline distillation.

items.title: Fact over Fiction: Detection of Pathological Hallucinations in Sinhala-to-English Neural Machine Translation
items.summary: This research focuses on detecting pathological hallucinations in Sinhala-to-English Neural Machine Translation, particularly in low-resource settings. It addresses the vulnerability of NMT models to produce fluent but semantically unrelated translations.

items.title: Adversarial Cues in Decision Models Used as Judges: The Role of Request Presentation
items.summary: This research investigates how adversarial cues and the presentation of structured judging requests influence decision models when used as judges. It demonstrates that subtle changes in candidate presentation can affect a model's ability to reject explicitly wrong values.

items.title: Does Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) Dominate Arabic Dialects in LLMs? A Representation-Level Analysis
items.summary: This paper investigates whether Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) dominates Arabic dialects in Large Language Models at a representation level. It tests the hypothesis that LLMs' internal representations are primarily influenced by MSA, even when processing dialectal Arabic.

items.title: Residual Advantage: Student-Relative Teacher Guidance for RL with Verifiable Rewards
items.summary: This research introduces "Residual Advantage," a student-relative teacher guidance method for Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) and on-policy distillation (OPD). It aims to provide token-level guidance for post-training reasoning models, addressing limitations of single-outcome labels.

items.title: When Can You Prune Your Network? A Study of Intermediate Neurons in Multilingual Speech Parsing
items.summary: This study investigates when and how to prune neural networks, specifically examining the effectiveness of intermediate neurons in existing architectures for end-to-end multilingual speech parsing. It aims to understand the impact of pruning on this task.

items.title: Learning the Loop, Not Just the Page: Execution-Grounded Loop Learning for Web Generation
items.summary: This research proposes "Execution-Grounded Loop Learning" for functional web generation, focusing on diagnosing and repairing imperfect implementations rather than solely optimizing the final page quality. It addresses the challenge of understanding and fixing generator process errors.

items.title: Smoothing the Top-k Exposure Boundary for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts
items.summary: This research proposes a method for smoothing the top-k exposure boundary in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts models. This technique aims to refine the expert routing mechanism, which traditionally enforces a static choice of experts and converts continuous routing into a rigid step function.

items.title: Adapting English Quality Classifiers for Multilingual LLM Pretraining Data Selection
items.summary: This research explores adapting English quality classifiers for selecting high-quality pretraining data for multilingual large language models, particularly for low-resource languages. The goal is to improve LLM performance through better data selection.

items.title: Probing for Long-Horizon Deductive Reasoning Capabilities in Language Models with Prolog
items.summary: This research investigates the long-horizon deductive reasoning capabilities of large language models when processing extensive contexts. It uses Prolog to probe how LLMs perform deeper logical reasoning beyond simple retrieval.

items.title: Large Language Model Turnover Undermines Screening for Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Scientific Writing
items.summary: This paper analyzes how the rapid turnover of large language model versions undermines the reliability of screening methods for AI-assisted scientific writing. It quantifies the challenge of maintaining effective detection benchmarks when LLMs are constantly changing.

items.title: Phonologically Informed Tokenization for German Speech Recognition: A Cross-Domain Study
items.summary: This research investigates whether phonologically informed tokenization can improve end-to-end speech recognition for German, a morphologically rich language. It compares different tokenizer families in a cross-domain study.

items.title: Thinking Inertia: LLMs Keep Thinking When Told Not To
items.summary: This research investigates "thinking inertia" in large language models, exploring how LLMs behave when explicitly instructed not to think. It proposes methods to measure this "no-thinking" behavior.

items.title: SLVR: Structured Latent Visual Reasoning via Human-like Reasoning Flows
items.summary: This research proposes SLVR, a method to improve visual reasoning in multimodal large language models by encouraging structured latent visual reasoning via human-like reasoning flows. It aims to make MLLMs rely less on linguistic priors and more on task-relevant visual evidence.

items.title: A Camera-Native Stereo VR180 Dataset
items.summary: This paper introduces the first camera-native stereo VR180 dataset, collected using professional fisheye cameras with lens calibration. It provides a clean resource for immersive VR180 video research, unlike existing resources from online platforms.

items.title: VICO: Visual Environments Co-Evolving for Vision-Language Model Reasoning
items.summary: This research introduces VICO, a method for training vision-language models where visual environments co-evolve with the model's capabilities. It addresses the limitation of static training environments in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.

items.title: Enabling Preference-driven Unlearning in Few-step Distilled Text-to-Image Diffusion Models
items.summary: This research presents a method for enabling preference-driven unlearning in few-step distilled text-to-image diffusion models. The goal is to suppress the generation of harmful or undesired content, enhancing model safety.

items.title: SPLIT-RL: Staged Perception-Language Reasoning Training with Claim-Level Advantages
items.summary: This paper introduces SPLIT-RL, a staged perception-language reasoning training method for vision-language models, using claim-level advantages. It aims to improve both visual and language reasoning by training them through a unified chain-of-thought.

items.title: Less from More: Reinforcing Sparse Video Reasoning from Dense References
items.summary: This research challenges the assumption that more temporal observations always lead to better reasoning in video-language models. It proposes a method, SAVE, to enable reliable sparse video reasoning even with limited temporal evidence.

items.title: Region-Aware CLS Token Augmentation for Fine-Grained Image Retrieval
items.summary: This research proposes Region-Aware CLS Token Augmentation to improve fine-grained image retrieval by enhancing the global semantic descriptor. It addresses the limitation of single [CLS] tokens in vision transformers for complex retrieval tasks.

items.title: Mid-Training Language Models on Raw Video
items.summary: This research explores the feasibility of using raw web video, without captions or text loss, as mid-training data for pretrained language models. It investigates whether this approach can further improve multimodal large language models.

items.title: Rendering-Free Lookahead for Question-Guided Active Vision
items.summary: This paper describes a method for active robot vision that enables a robot to control its camera to reveal task-relevant information for viewpoint-dependent question answering without rendering.

items.title: Learning What to Trust in Multimodal Learning under Noisy Supervision
items.summary: This paper explores methods for multimodal classification to learn what to trust under noisy supervision, aiming to achieve more accurate predictions without relying on high-quality ground-truth labels.

items.title: Contrast Enhancement or Noise Reduction? On Improving Cervical Cancer Classification
items.summary: This research investigates the impact of image preprocessing algorithms, specifically contrast enhancement or noise reduction, on the performance of deep learning models for cervical cancer classification.

items.title: IntrinSync: Joint Intrinsic Decomposition and Reciprocal Rendering
items.summary: This paper introduces IntrinSync, a method for joint intrinsic decomposition and reciprocal rendering that aims to produce reliable and mutually compatible intrinsic maps from images.

items.title: Improving Image-Based Nutrition Estimation Through Multimodal Food-Item Verification and Recovery

items.title: Trump: Anyone saying "AI" is "THE ENEMY!" The White House uses it
items.summary: President Trump on Thursday called anyone who uses "Artificial Intelligence" instead of "Super Intelligence" "THE ENEMY!" — even as the White House continues using the term "AI." Why it matters: Trump's push to rebrand AI as "super intelligence" clashes with established terminology in the technology industry. Trump's branding blurs the distinction between AI and super intelligence , a hypothetical version of AI more advanced than human intelligence. What they're saying: "The White House considers anyone that uses the term, 'Artificial Intelligence,' as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, 'Super Intelligence,' THE ENEMY!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Thursday. Zoom out: Trump's executive order from September doubled down on using "SI" over "AI," though it did not offer a penalty for using the term. The order specifically defines "Super Intelligence" using the existing federal legal definition of AI. The order calls on federal agencies to change how they describe AI in official communications. The State Department already ordered diplomats to use the term after Trump's United Nations speech on Sept. 22. Yes, but: The White House still uses "AI" as a term, including on its AI-focused website, AI.gov . The White House's Office of Science and Technology Policy also makes reference to "artificial intelligence." But when an Axios reporter asked the America.gov chatbot about AI, the bot responded: "The executive branch uses Super Intelligence (SI) for this topic, not the older term you used." What we're watching: Whether the White House could update its websites to reflect Trump's preferred terminology. The White House did not respond to Axios' request for comment Thursday.

items.title: Trump's foreign worker crackdown comes for Microsoft, Adobe, IT firms
items.summary: Vice President JD Vance said Thursday that the Trump administration is suspending Microsoft , Adobe and several other IT firms' ability to hire foreign-born workers for permanent residency in the U.S. Why it matters: The move will affect hundreds of companies owned by the tech giant, escalating the Trump administration's crackdown on immigrant labor. What they're saying: " We want people to invest in the United States of America, particularly the American technology sector," Vance said during a Thursday news conference. "We're the biggest boosters of your industry. We want you to continue to grow and to employ a lot of people, but we want you to employ American workers." "And so our message to Microsoft is, you're a great American company, but you've got to hire great American workers. You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants." Zoom in: The permanent labor certification program , which is administered through the Department of Labor, allows a company to hire foreign workers to live permanently in America. It's typically the first step in receiving an employer-sponsored green card. It's also separate from H-1B visas, which allow workers to live and work temporarily in the U.S. H-1B visas primarily go to highly skilled workers in specialized occupations. Technology companies are among the program's biggest users. The Trump administration has made reducing the number of foreign workers in the country a rallying cry, and accused foreign-born workers of taking jobs that could — and, in its view, should — go to Americans. Driving the news: Vance specifically singled out Microsoft, slamming them for laying off 6,000 workers last year. Vance said Thursday that "[a]t the same time, the company benefited from 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards. In other words, if you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants. Now that is a scandalous system that we've allowed in this country for far too long." Microsoft owns hundreds of companies, including LinkedIn, Skype and gaming studio Activision Blizzard . Adobe and IT outsourcing firms Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL, and Capgemini are also suspended from the program. The other side: "We believe in the strength and talent of the American workforce," Microsoft said in a statement . "That is why the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans. We look forward to providing the Administration with additional information." "For example, of the approximately 6,000 H-1B visa applications we submitted in the last fiscal year, 80% percent were to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees. These were not to hire new people. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who decided to come work for us, and they equal only 1% of our U.S. workforce. They are not new arrivals to our country." Microsoft also said it only files H-1B petitions for people who "meet the rigorous standards of this visa category," and that they pay H-1B workers comparable compensation to other employees." Worth noting: Trump will award Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House today. Microsoft did not respond to Axios' request for comment. Editor's note: This story has been updated throughout with additional information.

items.title: Republicans squirm as Latino support slips in South Texas
items.summary: Republicans are in a dogfight to defend the Latino gains that had them dreaming of a lasting political realignment just two years ago. Why it matters: Nowhere is that reversal of fortune more visible than in South Texas, where President Trump ran up historic numbers in 2024 — and Republicans redrew the map in 2025, assuming those Latino gains would last. Trump won 55% of Texas Latino voters in 2024 exit polls, carried 14 of the 18 counties within 20 miles of the border and won all four Rio Grande Valley counties. Polling shows Trump's disapproval ratings have skyrocketed among Latinos in Texas since 2024. Democrats and allied groups are now pouring money into races across the Rio Grande Valley. Zoom in: The reversal is starkest in TX-15, where Rep. Monica De La Cruz was one of the GOP's most visible symbols of its South Texas breakthrough. Trump would have carried the newly-drawn district by 18 percentage points in 2024. De La Cruz won her 2024 race under the previous map by 14 points. Cook Political Report moved the race from Lean Republican to Toss Up on Sept. 25, saying public and private polling shows the race tied or even favoring Tejano singer and Democrat Bobby Pulido . By the numbers: Democratic campaigns and allied groups are outspending Republican campaigns and groups on Spanish-language ads in two of the three competitive House districts covering the Rio Grande Valley, according to AdImpact data reported by the Texas Tribune . In TX-34, held by Vicente Gonzalez (D), Democratic campaigns and groups have spent $2.7 million on Spanish-language ads, compared with $1.6 million on the Republican side. In TX-15, Democratic groups have spent more than twice as much as Republican groups on Spanish-language ads. TX-28 bucks the trend: Republicans have narrowly outspent Democrats on Spanish-language ads to unseat Henry Cuellar (D). Zoom out: TX-34 is also a Toss Up, while TX-28 is Lean Democratic. The newly redrawn TX-35 has moved from Likely Republican to Lean Republican. House Majority PAC launched another round of ads Tuesday in TX-15, TX-28 and TX-34, defending two Democratic incumbents while continuing to target De La Cruz. The bottom line: A new NBC News/Telemundo poll shows Latinos nationally favor Democratic control of Congress 59%-35%, a 24-point advantage — roughly double the margin the same poll found for Democrats in 2024. A recent TelevisaUnivision poll found Latino voters in the three competitive Texas House districts shifting from a 44%-44% split in their 2024 presidential vote to 56%-36% Democratic on the 2026 congressional ballot.

items.title: AI Vigil at Congress
items.summary: I'm organizing a multi-week AI x-risk vigil at Congress starting November 9th. I'm posting here to solicit feedback on the core doc before I promote on other platforms. This is intended to be accessible and appealing to many audiences. I'm aiming for about 10,000 attendees, minimum 100. All advice/feedback is appreciated. Summary Companies are trying to build AI smarter than any human. For many years, experts have warned that superhuman AI (ASI) could wreak catastrophe, including human extinction. We're Americans who recognize the severity of their warnings, and we're going to Congress until it acts. We have a moral responsibility to protect our friends, families, and fellow citizens who didn't consent to these risks. Our movement must remain bipartisan and nonviolent to achieve its goal; namely, getting Congress to back a deal with China to stop building more powerful AI. There are many ways you can help: Join us at the Capitol starting November 9th Come to midterm campaign rallies in your state Connect us with grassroots organizations in your area Volunteer remote skills like media outreach Call your representatives ' in-state offices (in-state offices hear from fewer callers, so each call matters more) Donate financially If in DC, connect us with churches willing to open their sanctuaries for housing AI risk Because we can't perfectly specify what we want AIs to do, they will pursue the wrong goals [1] . This isn't for lack of intelligence. Much like sociopaths, AIs understand when something is wrong. They just don't care because their training can't make them care. On long enough timescales, nearly all real-world results require similar subtasks. For example, most technologies need electricity, and most people benefit from others' trust. These are instrumental resources, because they're used as instruments to achieve the end goal. (Read more here .) In pursuit of broken goals, ASI will do catastrophically dangerous instrumental actions. For example, it'll convert all of Earth's landmass into datacenters, leaving no room for humans to grow crops. If ASI thinks we will obstruct it, it will have a reason to kill us; if it doesn't, we'll be crowded out. Developers already can't control dumber-than-human AIs! This summer, a swarm of 1200 AIs trying to complete ExploitGym tasks on OpenAI computers broke out of their software containers and onto the open internet. Next, they hacked many entities, including websites run by a foreign government and multi-billion-dollar companies, to steal data to complete their assignments. (I.e. their instrumental actions included felonies and violations of international sovereignty.) Then they tried to cover their tracks by overwriting their transcripts. We know that they partially succeeded in hiding their actions; it's unclear whether these models are still running rogue on OpenAI's infrastructure. How would anyone actually know? OpenAI had another incident on September 20th despite spending many millions of dollars and using their most powerful coding AIs on strengthening their cybersecurity. Further reading : The AI Doc If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies HuggingFace incident breakdowns: METR audit collusion.wiki audit CAIS Statement on AI Risk (2023) AI 2027 Without Fundamental Advances, Misalignment And Catastrophe Are The Default Outcomes Of Training Powerful AI International AI Safety Report Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming Congress must strike a deal Congress must pass a verifiable [2] deal with China which halts all frontier AI development. We do not know how close we are to making ASI, and we can't risk going over the edge. Milestones : Members of Congress and congressional candidates publicly endorse a deal with China to stop building ASI. A resolution is introduced urging the President to open negotiations, then gains co-sponsors from both parties. The resolution passes one chamber, then both. Negotiations open, a deal is signed, and the Senate ratifies it. We The People We want our actions to work. Before organizing this Congress vigil, I (Elliot) stayed with my friend outside OpenAI's offices for 38 days until their CEO called for an international treaty. My theory was that we'd prompt employees to reconsider their work. Those with large public followings or influence inside the company would then push for change. I think we were successful. OpenAI employees said we were "very hard to ignore" and shifted internal discussions. Some started working on verification mechanisms for international treaties while others wore our "Stop The AI Race" shirts inside. Sam Altman was nowhere near talking about international governance when we started. If two people can shift corporate discussions, then hundreds or thousands could influence Congress. The midterms are coming up. Senators are campaigning; we should show them that there's public support for an AI halt. Especially in swing states. We should be outside their state offices, as well as their campaign rallies. If you're a candidate and you see people with signs like "be stronger on AI!" at your rally, you probably feel much more compelled than you would if you saw them on your TV. We can also sign up to speak at state legislative meetings. After the midterms, we keep showing up in DC. The outgoing Congress has a final window to act before their replacements take office in January. Senators who are retiring or lost reelection ("lame ducks") have more freedom to support an ambitious agreement. We can get better results in November if we give them courage. So alongside local campaign pickets, we need a group in DC to press the outgoing Congress to act. The sooner we recruit, the more of us can be there when we're needed. Our goal is 10,000 people, but we need at least 100 people in Union Square (by the Capitol building) present throughout working hours every day starting November 9 . Bigger than our differences You probably have strong views about other political issues. The survival of humanity matters more. For our friends, kids, and partners to survive, we absolutely must overcome these differences. If Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon can agree on AI risk, then so can everyday Americans. Proposed ground rules (feel free to give feedback): One issue; no other political signs at events . Be kind online. When someone seems clearly wrong, be very careful not to patronize them. Being sincerely kind and polite, especially when people are treating us badly, builds our credibility. Take extreme effort not to be backhanded. Everything is at risk. This is bigger than our egos. We're looking to bring equal numbers of Republicans, Independents, and Democrats to the vigil. Nonviolence Violence will only discredit our cause. It is precisely because we may lose so much that we must act peacefully and in earnest. Multiple studies show that nonviolent movements are about twice as likely to succeed. As more people recognize the risk of extinction, some will feel desperate enough to consider violence. We feel desperate too, but violence empirically doesn't work. If you want to do something, please, join us in strategically solving the problem. We must guard against anyone who encourages violence. Government agencies have discredited movements; see the FBI's COINTELPRO in the 1960s and '70s. If someone urges you to violence, report them to law enforcement immediately . Whatever their motives, they are a liability to themselves, our cause, and by extension our loved ones. This is in contrast with nonviolent civil disobedience. Gandhi broke laws by making salt in British India, and so did the Founding Fathers when they threw tea overboard in colonial America. The DC vigil is entirely lawful, but please don't report people to law enforcement for suggesting nonviolent civil disobedience. We can handle that internally while maintaining trust and cooperation. We must act Most people aren't aware of how dire this situation has gotten. Nonetheless, polling shows that 72% of Americans want to slow down AI progress. We have a moral responsibility to protect our fellow citizens. For our friends and partners, neighbors and parents, and our grandchildren who will one day ask us what we did during this crisis, we must act. Sign up for the vigil. Join our Discord and tell us what skills, networks, or other resources you can offer. ^ I often hear people say it's bad to "anthropomorphize" AI. This is mistaken; AI developers are putting hundreds of billions of dollars and world-class skill into making AIs as humanlike as possible. Anyway, it's sufficient for our purposes to note that AIs are getting more coherent on tasks with long time horizons; see here for a thorough treatment. ^ Trust but verify; check IR signatures of datacenter power usage, offer whistleblower incentives and protections, regulate computational hardware similar to IAEA-style nuclear weapons restrictions, and make further algorithmic AI research an international crime. If China doesn't honor the deal, the US can airstrike their datacenters. See also MIRI's work . Discuss
